title: Phrasal verbs 2: grammar and style
subtitle: turn it off, look after them, put sth off
summary: Learn where the object goes in a phrasal verb, and which formal single word means the same.

lesson.heading: Phrasal verbs with no object
lesson.text: Some phrasal verbs never take an object. You cannot put any words between the two parts.

examples.text: **Hold on**, I just need to get my coat.
The car **broke down** on my way to work.
There's nowhere for teenagers to go, so they just **hang around** on street corners.
examples.note: = spend time somewhere doing very little

lesson.heading: Separable phrasal verbs
lesson.text: Many phrasal verbs need an object, and the object can go in two places: after the verb, or between the two parts. These are called **separable** phrasal verbs.

examples.text: I **turned off** the lights in the living room.
examples.note: A long object usually goes at the end.

lesson.text: If the object is a pronoun (it, them, me, him), it must go in the middle: *Put them on.* (not ~~Put on them~~), *Take it off.* (not ~~Take off it~~).

lesson.heading: Phrasal verbs that cannot be separated
lesson.text: With some phrasal verbs the object must always come after both parts, even when it is a pronoun.

examples.text: I will **look after** the children for you.
How did the two men **break into** the shop?
examples.note: = enter using force, e.g. breaking a window

examples.text: It took her months to **get over** the shock.
examples.note: = begin to feel better after being unhappy or ill

examples.text: A girl was **handing out** leaflets at the station.
examples.note: = giving them to all the people in a group. This one is separable: handing them out.

lesson.heading: What a dictionary tells you
rows: They hang around on street corners.
the object can go in the middle
Hand out the books. / Hand them out.
the object must come after the phrasal verb
She got over the shock. / She got over it.

lesson.heading: Informal phrasal verb, formal single word
rows: He made a list of people but left me out.
We had to make up a story.
They put the game off till Friday.
I offered her a job but she turned it down.
Could you hold on a minute, please?
The train should get in by ten o'clock.

lesson.heading: Which one should I use?
lesson.text: Phrasal verbs are very common in spoken and written English, but many of them are quite informal. In a formal letter or report, the single word often sounds better.

examples.text: *Informal:* We've had to **put off** the meeting till next week.
*Formal:* The meeting has been **postponed** until next week.

exercises.prompt: She asked me to hand ___ at the station.
exercises.explanation: A pronoun object must go between the two parts: hand them out.

exercises.prompt: My boots were tight and I couldn't take ___.
exercises.explanation: Take them off. We never say take off them.

exercises.statement: Could you turn the light on?
exercises.explanation: Correct. Turn on is separable, so the light can go in the middle or at the end.

exercises.statement: They offered him the job, but why did they turn down it?
exercises.explanation: Why did they turn it down? A pronoun must go between the two parts.

exercises.statement: The boys were hanging the station around.
exercises.explanation: The boys were hanging around the station. Hang around takes no object between its parts.

exercises.prompt: Does the phrasal verb take an object or not?
Match each formal word with the informal phrasal verb that means the same.
As so many people are ill, I've had to ___ the meeting till next week.
The teacher told us to ___ a story to go with the picture.
exercises.explanation: Make something up = create it from your imagination.

exercises.prompt: We didn't think Mike was good enough, so we left him ___.
exercises.explanation: Leave someone out = not include them.

exercises.prompt: He told me he was 25, but I don't believe him. I think he's making that ___.
We'll get there by seven if we set ___ now.
I'll call ___ you a bit later. I should be at your house by 7 o'clock.
exercises.explanation: Call for someone = go to collect them.
